newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland opens EU information centre, hotline.
newsitem.headline: Poland opens EU information centre, hotline.

text.p: Poland's government on Monday launched an EU Information Centre with relays of specially-trained students fielding calls from citizens wondering what membership of the bloc will mean for them.

"This is where one can get comprehensive, detailed competent information on everything regarding our aspirations towards the European Union, our preparations for membership and for negotiations," Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told a news conference after the opening in Warsaw. @
The centre will employ 40 university students on subjects related to EU entry, taking turns to staff 10 lines and computers working six days a week, 12 hours a day on weekdays.

They will be able to refer questions to experts and officials on the government European Integration Committee Office, which will launch its website this month (www.kprm.gov.pl/kie/cie/html) and is distributing more than 130,000 free brochures on aspects of the process.
Cimoszewicz said there was huge support for EU entry, shown by polls at more than 70 percent, based on what he said was a justified expectation that it would be good for Poland. @
"But it is also true that without wider discussion there is less knowledge of the price that we will have to pay for entering the union," he said.
Cimoszewicz said Poland now expected the EU would conclude its current inter-government conference on time so that Poland and other aspirants could begin talks in early 1998.

He said many of 30 inter-ministerial teams called to draft Poland's negotiating strategies on specific issues would produce initial reports within weeks, but these would be kept strictly confidential so as not to reveal Poland's hand. @

Danuta Huebner, cabinet minister in charge of European integration, said that when the telephone information line started operations on Friday ahead of the launch it got 400 enquiries of which two-thirds were from outside Warsaw.
Although main political parties are all in favour of EU entry, some influential voices argue against haste and saying Poland should hold out for the best possible deal.

Such arguments are gaining in the Polish Peasant party, smaller partner of Cimoszewicz's ex-communists in the ruling coalition, and in the rightist opposition, especially the radical Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland (ROP).

The fears of groups such as the many small farmers that adjustment for EU membership will cause excessively painful upheaval in the countryside look set to become a factor in the campaign for parliamentary elections due in September and the government is launching a major campaign to stimulate debate.
On Friday Cimoszewicz appointed a 68-member council of business leaders, politicians, trade unionists, journalists and other experts to advise during the negotiations.
